name: Kapaleeshwarar Temple, Mylapore
deity: Shiva, worshipped as Kapaleeshwarar, with the goddess Karpagambal
summary: In the heart of old Madras, the Kapaleeshwarar temple crowns the ancient quarter of Mylapore with a towering, sculpture-covered gopuram. Rebuilt in the Vijayanagara period after its seaside predecessor was lost, it is Chennai's best-loved Shiva temple and the stage each spring for the great Arupathimoovar procession.

sections.history: Mylapore is among the oldest inhabited parts of Chennai, and Tamil tradition counts the Kapaleeshwarar temple among the shrines sung by the seventh-century saints Appar and Sambandar in the Tevaram. The original temple is believed to have stood nearer the shore; by tradition that early shrine was lost during the reshaping of the coast in the sixteenth century, and the present temple was raised a little inland, in the Vijayanagara period, on the tank-side site it occupies today. The hymns of the Nayanars and later inscriptions tie the place to a deep Shaiva past, while the streets around it grew into a temple town of agraharams, weavers, and merchants. As the city of Madras rose around it, Mylapore kept this temple at its centre, and it remains the spiritual anchor of one of Chennai's most storied neighbourhoods.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered beneath a soaring eastern gopuram that rises about thirty-seven metres in vivid tiers of stucco figures — gods, saints, and mythic scenes repainted in bright colours every few years. Within the walls, granite pillared halls lead to the sanctum of Kapaleeshwarar and the shrine of the goddess Karpagambal, 'the goddess of the wish-granting tree.' A second, smaller gopuram stands over the western entrance beside the great temple tank. The spacious courtyard shelters a cluster of subsidiary shrines and a stone image of the goddess as a peahen worshipping the lingam, recalling the legend that gives Mylapore its name. Bronze processional deities, a festival mandapa, and inscriptions along the plinth round out a plan modest in footprint but rich in the layered density of a living city temple.
sections.legends: The name Mylapore comes from mayil, the Tamil word for peacock, and the temple's central legend explains why. Parvati, it is told, was distracted for a moment during Shiva's teaching, and to atone she came to this shore and worshipped him in the form of a peahen beneath a punnai tree; pleased, Shiva restored her, and the place became Mylai, the town of the peahen. A second beloved story belongs to the saint Sambandar: a merchant's daughter, Poompavai, died of snakebite before she could be wed, and her grieving father kept her ashes; when Sambandar came to Mylapore he sang over the urn, and the girl was restored as Poompavai, 'the maiden of flowers.' Both tales are retold at the temple to this day, kept close by the peahen shrine and Poompavai's memory.
sections.festivals: The temple's grandest season is the Panguni festival in March and April, and its most famous day is Arupathimoovar, when the bronze images of the sixty-three Nayanar saints are carried in a vast procession through the streets of Mylapore, drawing crowds from across the city. The Brahmotsavam around it fills nine or ten days with flag-hoisting, decorated temple cars, and great floral and silver mounts for the deities. Arudra Darisanam in the month of Margazhi, dear to Shiva as Nataraja, and the float festival on the temple tank are marked with particular beauty, the deities circling the lit water on a garlanded raft. Navaratri honours the goddess Karpagambal, and the pre-dawn Margazhi mornings fill the old streets with the singing of Tevaram.
sections.experience: To step from the bustle of Mylapore's market lanes into the Kapaleeshwarar temple is to meet the city's oldest rhythm. The great east gopuram, freshly painted, is a landmark above the rooftops; beneath it the courtyard opens cool and unhurried, scented with jasmine from the flower sellers at the gate. Devotees circle the sanctum, pause at Karpagambal's shrine, and rest along the pillared halls as bells and nadaswaram drift across the tank. Evenings are especially alive, when the lamps are lit and families arrive after the day's work, and during festivals the surrounding streets themselves become the temple. Even a first-time visitor senses that this is not a monument but a living heart, worshipped without interruption while the modern city grew up around it.

visit.timings: Generally open around 5:00 am to 12:00 pm and 4:00 pm to 9:00 pm daily, with extended hours and special processions during Panguni and other festivals.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is appreciated: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is removed before entering.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer courtyards and of the gopuram, but not inside the inner sanctum. Check with temple staff, as rules can change during festivals.
visit.gettingThere: Mylapore is in central Chennai, about 3 km from Chennai Egmore and well served by city buses, taxis, and app cabs; suburban rail and metro connections are a short ride away, and Chennai International Airport is roughly 15 km to the southwest.
